extracted.intended_audience: legal scholars, patent litigators, policymakers, and empirical researchers studying patent remedies
extracted.subtask_description: Empirical and doctrinal analysis of factors that predict whether U.S. district courts grant permanent injunctions in patent litigation, and the implications of eBay's four-factor test for different types of patentees.

rubrics_metrics.name: eBay four-factor test (entitlement to equitable relief)
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts determine entitlement to a permanent injunction under eBay’s four-factor test, which requires consideration of irreparable injury (first factor), inadequacy of remedies at law, balance of hardships, and the public interest (final factor).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper emphasizes that the first factor (irreparable injury) appears to be the main stumbling block for PAEs/non‑competitors, and that the final eBay factor (public interest) has driven denials in medical device cases where injunctive relief would disserve public health or access. The Supreme Court cautioned against categorical rules denying injunctions to broad classes of patentees; courts should apply traditional equitable principles on a case-by-case basis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competitor status of patentee (COMPETE)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the patentee and infringer were competitors is a primary factor related to injunctive relief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This variable is the single most significant predictor in the models; it is highly statistically significant (p < 0.001) with large odds ratios (e.g., 13.49 in Model #1 rising to 27.68 in Model #3), and its predictive power increases as controls are added. Courts commonly award injunctions to operating companies that compete with the infringer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentee type: PAE (patent assertion entity) status
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the patentee is a PAE (non‑practicing or patent assertion entity) affects the likelihood of obtaining a permanent injunction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PAE status is statistically significant in the expected direction in the final model (fewer injunctions granted to PAEs). However, there is collinearity between PAE and COMPETE (PAEs typically do not compete), which probably leads models to underestimate the strength of the relationship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent claims a 'small component' (COMPONENT)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the asserted patent covers only a small component of the infringing product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a patent covers a small component, district courts rarely grant an injunction (district courts granted injunctions 14% of the time where a small component finding was made). This follows Justice Kennedy’s admonition to avoid injunctive relief when the patented invention is but a small component of the product.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentee’s willingness to license (LICENSE)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the patentee has shown willingness to license the patent(s)-in-suit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrary to some expectations, willingness to license is positively correlated with injunctive relief after controlling for other factors in the models, though this finding is not statistically significant (p = 0.125 in Model #3). Overall patentees who engaged in licensing were slightly less likely to obtain an injunction in raw rates (64% vs. 77%) but controls change the sign.

rubrics_metrics.name: Willful infringement finding (WILLFUL)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the court found the defendant’s infringement to be willful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A finding of willful infringement does not have a statistically significant correlation with permanent injunction decisions in the models reported.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technology category (industry/field of patent)
rubrics_metrics.description: The field of technology for the patent(s)-in-suit (e.g., software, electronics, electrical, mechanical, chemistry, drugs, medical device, Computers & Communications) influences injunction outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Biotechnology and pharmaceuticals receive injunctions at very high rates; medical devices show a significantly lower grant rate (often because public interest weighs against removing medical devices from the market); software/computers are negatively correlated with injunctions (the Computers & Communications NBER category was negatively correlated). The paper stresses that courts apply patent doctrines and remedies in a technology‑specific manner despite formal technology-neutrality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forum/district (venue) effects
rubrics_metrics.description: The district court in which the case is heard affects the likelihood of an injunction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Certain districts show statistically significant correlations with injunction grants/denials (e.g., District of Delaware negatively correlated with injunctive relief; Eastern District of Texas produced three of four PAE injunctions). These differences create potential incentives for forum shopping and support arguments for venue-limiting reforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measured patent characteristics (CLAIMS, PRIORART, PARENT, FWDCITEPERYEAR, PROSECUTIONYEAR, SMALL_ENTITY, ISSUE2INJUNCTION)
rubrics_metrics.description: Observable patent-level variables hypothesized to predict patent value and therefore injunctive relief: number of claims, prior art citations, parent-family size, forward citations per year, time in prosecution, small entity status, and time between issue and injunction decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior literature suggested positive correlations with value (and thus with injunctions). In the Patents Dataset regression, none of these measured patent characteristics had a statistically significant relationship with injunction outcomes; the only patent-related control that was significant was the Computers & Communications technology category. Odds ratios close to 1 were reported (e.g., CLAIMS .998).

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical evaluation metrics and methodology (logistic regression interpretation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of logistic (logit) regression to measure relationships between independent variables and the dependent variable (injunction granted); report of odds ratios, standard errors, p-values/asterisks for significance, and pseudo‑R2 as measure of model predictive power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Odds ratios >1 indicate positive association with injunction entry; <1 indicate negative association; odds ratios reported to two decimal places. Significance indicated by * p<0.05, ** p<0.01, *** p<0.001. Pseudo‑R2 values (reported in final row) range 0–1 and higher values indicate better model fit. The authors cite UCLA ATS FAQs for interpreting odds ratios and pseudo‑R2s.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public interest as an eBay factor (final factor examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: The public interest factor can militate against injunctive relief where an injunction would disserve public health or access (e.g., removing medical devices or contact lenses from the market would harm patients/consumers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper cites multiple district court opinions declining to award injunctions for medical devices and other products on public interest grounds (e.g., potential risk to patient health, millions of contact lens wearers suffering adverse consequences). These concrete examples show how public interest considerations have reduced injunction rates in certain technologies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technology‑specific application of doctrines (technology bias)
rubrics_metrics.description: Although patent law is formally technology-neutral, courts apply doctrines (e.g., nonobviousness, enablement, written description) and remedies in a technology-specific manner, affecting injunction outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors cite literature arguing that doctrines and remedies vary by field (biotechnology and pharmaceuticals more likely to get injunctions; software less). This technology‑specificity is identified as a systematic influence on injunction decisions and is relevant to normative assessment and policy reform.

rubrics_metrics.name: Normative/policy considerations regarding liability vs. property rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Post-eBay, a bifurcated system of property rules (injunctions for competitors) and liability rules (money damages for many non-practicing entities) has emerged, with normative implications for innovation incentives and patent value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Denying injunctive relief to PAEs may prevent rent‑seeking nuisance settlements but may also harm startups and innovators that rely on exclusion rights to commercialize inventions; loss of the right to exclude can reduce bargaining power and licensing rates. The paper discusses tradeoffs and empirical evidence (e.g., venture-backed firms’ reliance on patents).
